sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Cheírōn** (*cheiron*) — Wisdom, Teaching, Heroes · The wisest of the centaurs, tutor of heroes (Achilles, Asklepios, Iason, Herakles); the name is traditionally linked to Greek χείρ ("hand"), though its true origin is uncertain — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Wisdom, Teaching, Heroes". The name means "The wisest of the centaurs, tutor of heroes (Achilles, Asklepios, Iason, Herakles); the name is traditionally linked to Greek χείρ ("hand"), though its true origin is uncertain"[^1].

Cheírōn is the exception among the wild **κένταυροι**: the immortal son of Kronos who dwells in a cave on Mount Pelion and turns raw princes into heroes. Where his kin are drunkards and rapine, Homer calls him **δικαιότατος Κενταύρων** — the most just of centaurs. He is the teacher: medicine for **Asklepios**, the lyre and the remedies for **Achilles**, the whole heroic craft for Iason and Herakles.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Cheírōn** and serves its temple at [cheírōn.com](https://xn--chern-1sa78d.com). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *cheiron* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Greek as **Χείρων**. Etymologically it means "The wisest of the centaurs, tutor of heroes (Achilles, Asklepios, Iason, Herakles); the name is traditionally linked to Greek χείρ ("hand"), though its true origin is uncertain"[^1].

The ASCII form *cheiron* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Cheírōn** recovers both the stress accent and the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **c** → **C** — C uppercase
- **h** → **h** — h same
- **e** → **e** — e same
- **i** → **í** — Acute on i
- **r** → **r** — r same
- **o** → **ō** — Macron on o
- **n** → **n** — n same

The project holds the domain **cheírōn.com** (xn--chern-1sa78d.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/kʰéː.rɔːn/** — Attic Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Kh-** — aspirated k (χ), a hard stop released with a strong breath — not the fricative of modern Greek
- **-eí-** — long close ē (ει), carrying the high pitch of the acute accent
- **-rōn** — long open ō (ω) with final n

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'KHEH-rōn' — long ē, long ō, the pitch rising on the first syllable

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — χείρ (kheír), 'hand' — the traditional association of the name, possibly a folk etymology
- **PIE** — if the link holds, χείρ descends from PIE *ǵʰésr- 'hand' (cf. Hittite keššar); the name's own derivation remains uncertain — Beekes treats the connection cautiously

Tier 1: the Greek original Χείρων carries both stress (the acute on ει) and long vowels (ει and ω). The restored form Cheírōn preserves both marks — the accent and the macron — that plain ASCII 'Cheiron' erases.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Cheírōn concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The Pelian Ash Spear** — The great spear of ash wood that Cheírōn cut on Pelion's peak and gave to Peleus at his wedding — the same spear Achilles alone could wield (Iliad 16.143–144). The teacher's gift that arms the hero.
- **The Cave on Mount Pelion** — His dwelling and school, the legendary academy of heroes where the gods themselves celebrated the wedding of Peleus and Thetis (Pindar, Pythian 9.29–30).
- **The Lyre** — The instrument of the education he gave Achilles, who in Iliad 9 (186–189) is found in his hut singing the glories of heroes to the lyre.
- **Herbs and Remedies (φάρμακα)** — The healing lore he taught Asklepios and gave to Peleus's line; Achilles treats wounds with remedies 'that Cheiron gave his father' (Iliad 4.219, 11.831–832).
- **The Hydra-Poisoned Arrow** — Herakles's stray arrow, dipped in the Lernaean hydra's venom, that struck his knee and gave the immortal an unhealable wound (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4).
- **The Stars** — Zeus set him in the sky — remembered as Centaurus or Sagittarius — after he surrendered his immortality and died (Ovid, Fasti 5.379–414; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Cheírōn stands at the hinge of two orders: Titan-born yet honored by the Olympians, beast-bodied yet the very image of wisdom. His myths are the myths of transmission — what one generation hands to the next.[^1]

### Son of Kronos and Philyra (Birth)

Kronos lay with the Oceanid Philyra in the shape of a horse, and from that union was born a child of double nature — half god, half horse: *Apollodorus, Library* 1.2.4. Pindar likewise names him the son of Philyra and Kronos, making Cheírōn the **half-brother of Zeus** (*Pythian* 4.102–103). Abandoned by his mother, who in shame was changed into a linden tree in later telling, he was reared by Apollo and Artemis, from whom he learned the arts he would pass on. Thus the wisest of teachers begins as the child of deception and rejection.[^2]

### Tutor of the Heroes (The School of Pelion)

Pindar gives the roll of his pupils: in his cave Cheírōn reared **Iason**, gentle-handed **Asklepios**, whom he taught the craft of remedies, and **Achilles**, whom he fed on the marrow of lions and wild boars to make him fierce (*Nemean* 3.43–58). Homer twice seals the bond: Achilles carries remedies 'that Cheiron gave to his father in friendship' (*Iliad* 4.218–219), and is the man 'whom Cheiron taught, the most just of the centaurs' — *δικαιότατος Κενταύρων* (*Iliad* 11.831–832). Actaeon and Herakles also passed through his tutelage. In Pindar's grief for Hieron, the poet wishes Cheírōn still lived in his cave, that another healer might come to Sicily (*Pythian* 3.1–7).

### The Spear for Peleus (The Gift)

When Peleus married the sea-goddess Thetis, the wedding feast was held on Pelion at Cheírōn's cave, and the centaur gave the bridegroom a spear of mountain ash cut from Pelion's peak (*Iliad* 16.143–144). That spear passed to Achilles, and at Troy no other Achaean could wield it — Patroklos himself left it behind when he donned Achilles's armor, 'heavy, huge, and strong.' The teacher's gift thus runs through the whole *Iliad*: it is the one weapon that marks the hero he made. The marriage it honored also produced the child Cheírōn would raise.

### The Immortal Who Chose Death (The Wound and the Stars)

When Herakles fought the wild centaurs at the cave of Pholos, one of his arrows — tipped with the hydra's incurable venom — struck Cheírōn's knee (*Apollodorus, Library* 2.5.4). The poison that the great healer had no remedy for burned in his own flesh; immortal, he could neither heal nor die. Sophocles remembers the shaft as the one 'wherewith Cheiron was struck' (*Trachiniae* 714–716). At last he surrendered his immortality and was allowed to die, and Zeus set him among the stars — Ovid watches the father of heroes' education take his place in the sky (*Fasti* 5.379–414; cf. Hyginus, *Astronomica* 2.38). The teacher's last lesson is mortality itself.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Rome changed Cheírōn least of all the Greek figures: he keeps his name as **Chiron** in Latin, too singular to be merged with any Italian power. What Rome absorbed was his catasterism — Latin poets and star-cataloguers fixed him in the sky, debating whether the Centaurus or the Sagittarius was his (Ovid, *Fasti* 5; Hyginus, *Astronomica* 2.38). In later tradition he remains the named exception among his kind: Dante makes him chief of the centaurs who guard the violent in *Inferno* 12, still 'Chiron, who nursed Achilles.' The word 'centaur' (κένταυρος) traveled into every European language, but Cheírōn travels as himself.[^1]

Within the Greek tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], [[aer|Aḗr]], [[aither|Aithḗr]], and [[ananke|Anánkē]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: His name lives in the sky: the minor planet **2060 Chiron**, discovered in 1977 between Saturn and Uranus, was named for him and gave its class of objects — the **centaurs**, bodies orbiting among the giant planets — their collective name. Modern astrology adopted him as the emblem of the **wounded healer**, the one whose incurable hurt becomes the source of healing for others. Ancient herbalists named the plant **centaury** (κενταύριον, Centaurium) after the centaur's healing lore. And the old association of his name with χείρ, the hand, echoes — though by the word's own root, not by his name — in 'surgery,' from χειρουργία, 'hand-work.'[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: No great temple of Cheírōn is known; he is a daimonic tutor, not an Olympian with a state cult, though a cave above Portaria on Mount Pelion is traditionally identified as the Cheironeion, his school. His real monument is the art: Attic black- and red-figure vases repeatedly show Peleus handing the infant Achilles into the centaur's arms, and Roman sarcophagi of the 'education of Achilles' (2nd–3rd c. CE) show him teaching the lyre. The sculpted centauromachies — the Olympia west pediment and the Parthenon south metopes — preserve the wild centaur type against which his justice was defined.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Cheírōn is the Greek answer to a question the centauromachy asks in stone at Olympia and on the Parthenon: can nature be educated? He is a κένταυρος — the very type of ungoverned appetite — who is instead called *most just*. That he is Kronos's son and Zeus's half-brother matters: he belongs to the older, Titan order, yet serves the new one by raising its heroes, as if the wild past could be redeemed only by becoming a teacher. His unhealable wound completes the thought — the master of remedies cannot master his own pain, and immortality becomes not a privilege but a sentence. That he must surrender deathlessness to find release is among the most quietly radical moments in Greek myth: even an immortal may long for the human portion.[^1]
